# 6.1 Bird's-Eye View of RD

## Where we left off

- Lecture 3 ended on a trade. **Matching** needs common support; **regression** needs a correctly specified outcome model and will extrapolate where the data are silent.
- In regression discontinuity, at any value of the running variable, you observe treated units **or** control units. Overlap is exactly zero.
- So extrapolation is the entire design. The question becomes: *how short a distance can we extrapolate, and how honestly?*
- The answer --- extrapolate to a **point**, from both sides --- is what makes RD a credible observational design we have. 

<!--
## Sixty years old, and suddenly everywhere

- **Thistlethwaite and Campbell (1960).** Merit awards assigned on a test-score cutoff; they compared students just above and just below. The design was there, fully formed, in 1960 --- invented by an educational psychologist.
- **Goldberger (1972)** discussed it. Economics ignored it for another 27 years: too niche, too specialised.
- **1999, two papers in the *QJE*.** Angrist and Lavy used Israeli class-size rules that mechanically split classes past a threshold. Black used school-district boundaries --- the first "spatial RD".
- **Lee and Lemieux (2010)** in the *JEL*, plus *Mostly Harmless Econometrics*, made it standard.
- What actually made it spread: **administrative data**. RD needs many observations packed around one point, and that is exactly what registry data provide.
-->

## The intuition: drinking at 21

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 2.8
RED <- "#B2182B"; BLU <- "#2166AC"
set.seed(21)
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4.2, 2.2, 1), cex = 0.8)

## --- stylised: share of days drinking -------------------------------------
ag <- seq(19, 23, by = 1/12)
f  <- function(a) 6.6 + 0.62*(a - 19) - 0.02*(a - 19)^2
sh <- f(ag) + 1.9*(ag >= 21) + rnorm(length(ag), 0, 0.22)
plot(ag, sh, pch = 16, cex = 0.6, col = "grey35", xlab = "age",
     ylab = "share of days drinking (%)", main = "Drinking behaviour", ylim = c(6, 12))
abline(v = 21, lty = 2, col = "grey45")
for (s in 0:1) {
  k  <- if (s == 0) ag < 21 else ag >= 21
  dd <- data.frame(a = ag[k], y = sh[k])
  m  <- lm(y ~ poly(a, 2, raw = TRUE), data = dd)
  aa <- seq(min(dd$a), max(dd$a), length.out = 100)
  lines(aa, predict(m, data.frame(a = aa)), col = if (s == 0) BLU else RED, lwd = 2.4)
}

## --- stylised: motor-vehicle mortality ------------------------------------
g  <- function(a) 35 - 2.4*(a - 19) + 0.25*(a - 19)^2
mo <- g(ag) + 5*(ag >= 21) + rnorm(length(ag), 0, 0.7)
plot(ag, mo, pch = 16, cex = 0.6, col = "grey35", xlab = "age",
     ylab = "deaths per 100,000", main = "Motor-vehicle mortality", ylim = c(27, 40))
abline(v = 21, lty = 2, col = "grey45")
for (s in 0:1) {
  k  <- if (s == 0) ag < 21 else ag >= 21
  dd <- data.frame(a = ag[k], y = mo[k])
  m  <- lm(y ~ poly(a, 2, raw = TRUE), data = dd)
  aa <- seq(min(dd$a), max(dd$a), length.out = 100)
  lines(aa, predict(m, data.frame(a = aa)), col = if (s == 0) BLU else RED, lwd = 2.4)
}
```

\vspace{-0.3em}
\footnotesize
Drinking rises at 21 because that is when it becomes legal. Motor-vehicle mortality falls steadily with age, then jumps back up at exactly the same point.


## What makes it an RD figure

Three elements, and every RD figure has all three:

1. **The dots.** Average outcomes within narrow bins of the running variable --- here, one dot per month of age. Not raw observations.
2. **The lines.** Fitted values from a regression, estimated **separately on each side** of the cutoff. The curvature comes from a polynomial in age.
3. **The break.** That gap is the whole estimate.

\vspace{0.3em}

- The break exists only because two different models were fit. Nothing forces them to meet --- so if they do meet, there is no effect.
- **The magnitude.** Roughly $5$ extra deaths per $100{,}000$ at age 21. With about $4.3$ million 21-year-olds in the US, that is $5 \times 43 \approx \mathbf{215}$ additional deaths a year attributable to legal drinking.
<!-- - Two figures, one story: drinking jumps, and so does the thing drinking causes.-->

## The jargon

- **Running variable** ($X$): the score that assigns treatment. Age, a test score, a credit score, a vote share, a BAC reading. Ideally continuous; a fine enough grid will do.
- **Cutoff** or **threshold** ($c_0$): the known value where assignment changes.
- **Trends**: how the *outcome* moves with the running variable --- **not** time trends. In the mortality figure, deaths fall with age; that is an outcome trend.
- **Discontinuity** or **jump**: the break in the conditional mean at $c_0$. That break is the estimate.
- The design is named for the discontinuity, but it lives or dies on the **trends**. Strong trends make effects hard to detect and easy to manufacture. 

## Where do running variables come from?

- They sound exotic. They are everywhere, because **humans write rules**, and rules need thresholds.
- **Governments**: Medicare at 65, the drinking age at 21, adult criminal liability at 18, income thresholds for transfer programs.
- **Firms and markets**: credit-score cutoffs in lending, index membership rules, covenant thresholds, EPS targets in compensation contracts, a $50\%$ vote share.
- **Algorithms**: surge pricing, credit limits, automated underwriting. 
- Finding one requires **institutional knowledge**, not econometrics. Knowing the rule exists, and exactly how it is applied, is the hard part.

## And RD needs a great deal of data

- The estimate comes from observations **near the cutoff**. Everything else only helps pin down the two limits.
- So the binding constraint is not the number of rows in your dataset. It is the number of rows in a neighbourhood of one point.
- Strong trends make this worse: the more steeply the outcome moves with $X$, the more data you need to separate the jump from the slope.
- This is why RD studies are overwhelmingly built on **administrative records** --- birth registries, school records, court records, credit bureaus.
- It is also why RD in finance is often underpowered. We return to this.

# 6.2 Identification Assumptions


## Sharp and fuzzy

\begin{center}
\small
\begin{tabular}{lll}
\toprule
 & Sharp & Fuzzy \\
\midrule
$\Pr(D = 1 \mid X)$ at $c_0$ & jumps $0 \to 1$ & jumps, but not to $1$ \\
Treatment is       & a deterministic function of $X$ & influenced by $X$ \\
The cutoff is      & the assignment rule & an \emph{instrument} \\
Example            & Medicare at $65$ & Israeli class-size rules \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

- We do the **sharp** design here. The fuzzy design is an instrumental-variables problem, so it waits for the IV lecture.
- Many finance applications are fuzzy. A shareholder proposal that passes with $51\%$ is not always implemented.

## The sharp design

In a sharp RD, treatment status is a **deterministic, discontinuous** function of the running variable:
$$
D_i = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } X_i \geq c_0 \\ 0 & \text{if } X_i < c_0 \end{cases}
$$

- Know $X_i$ and you know $D_i$ with certainty. Know someone's age and their country, and you know whether they may legally drink.
- Contrast the fuzzy design, where crossing $c_0$ raises $\Pr(D=1)$ without driving it to one.
<!-- - Medicare at 65 is the textbook sharp case --- setting aside early eligibility through disability.-->

## The key feature: no common support

- This is a selection-on-observables design: condition on $X$ and treatment is fully determined, so **unconfoundedness holds trivially**.
- But the other assumption of Lecture 3 fails completely. At any value of $X$ you see treated units or controls, never both:
$$
e(X) = \Pr(D = 1 \mid X) \in \{0, 1\} \quad \text{everywhere.}
$$
- No 19-year-old may legally drink; every 21-year-old may. There is no overlap to exploit.
- **Every tool from last week is unusable.** You cannot match, stratify, or weight --- no unit has a counterpart at its own value of $X$.
- What replaces overlap is a **smoothness** assumption, plus a limiting argument at a single point.

## The target parameter

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 2.7
c0 <- 21; xs <- seq(19, 26, 0.05)
RED <- "#B2182B"; BLU <- "#2166AC"
YL <- c(7, 17)                       # a common scale, so the two gaps are comparable
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 2.2, 1), cex = 0.8)

## --- left: a constant effect of 4 ------------------------------------------
g0 <- function(x) 8 + 0.6*(x - 19)
g1 <- function(x) g0(x) + 4
plot(NULL, xlim = c(19, 26), ylim = YL, xlab = "age", ylab = "outcome",
     main = "Homogeneous effects")
abline(v = c0, lty = 2, col = "grey45")
lines(xs, g1(xs), col = RED, lwd = 2.2); lines(xs, g0(xs), col = BLU, lwd = 2.2)
arrows(c0, g0(c0), c0, g1(c0), code = 3, length = 0.04)
text(c0 + 0.2, (g0(c0) + g1(c0))/2, "4", adj = 0, cex = 0.85)
text(25.8, g1(25.8) + 0.55, expression(E*"["*Y^1*"|"*X*"]"), col = RED, cex = 0.75, adj = 1)
text(25.8, g0(25.8) - 0.75, expression(E*"["*Y^0*"|"*X*"]"), col = BLU, cex = 0.75, adj = 1)
text(22.6, 7.4, "the gap is 4 at every age", cex = 0.7, col = "grey25")

## --- right: 5.5 at 19, 2.35 at the cutoff, 0 at 23, negative after ---------
u  <- function(x) x - 19
h0 <- function(x) 8    + 0.900*u(x) - 0.02*u(x)^2
h1 <- function(x) 13.5 - 0.875*u(x) + 0.08*u(x)^2
plot(NULL, xlim = c(19, 26), ylim = YL, xlab = "age", ylab = "outcome",
     main = "Heterogeneous effects")
abline(v = c0, lty = 2, col = "grey45")
lines(xs, h1(xs), col = RED, lwd = 2.2); lines(xs, h0(xs), col = BLU, lwd = 2.2)
arrows(c0, h0(c0), c0, h1(c0), code = 3, length = 0.04)
text(c0 + 0.2, (h0(c0) + h1(c0))/2, "2.35", adj = 0, cex = 0.85)
points(23, h0(23), pch = 21, bg = "white", cex = 1.1, lwd = 1.6)
text(23, 9.7, "they cross at 23", cex = 0.7, col = "grey25")
text(19.2, h1(19.2) + 0.75, expression(E*"["*Y^1*"|"*X*"]"), col = RED, cex = 0.75, adj = 0)
text(19.2, h0(19.2) - 0.75, expression(E*"["*Y^0*"|"*X*"]"), col = BLU, cex = 0.75, adj = 0)
```

\vspace{-0.3em}
\footnotesize
Left: parallel potential outcomes, so the vertical gap is the same at every age and the number at the cutoff describes everyone. Right: the functions curve and **cross at 23** --- the effect is $5.5$ at age 19, $2.35$ at the cutoff, zero at 23, and *negative* beyond. RD returns the gap **at the dashed line** in both panels, and nothing else. 

## The estimand is a limit

$$
\tau \;=\; \underbrace{\lim_{x \downarrow c_0} E[Y_i \mid X_i = x]}_{\text{from the right}} \;-\; \underbrace{\lim_{x \uparrow c_0} E[Y_i \mid X_i = x]}_{\text{from the left}}
\;=\; E[Y^1_i - Y^0_i \mid X_i = c_0]
$$

- It is only *in the limit* that overlap is restored. Approaching $c_0$ from either side, the two groups become arbitrarily similar in $X$.
- This is an $ATE$, but for the subpopulation $\{X = c_0\}$ --- which is why it is often called a **local** average treatment effect.
- Note what it is **not**: not the $ATE$, not the $ATT$. It is an average at one point of one covariate.
- Data from a wide range of $X$ are used only to estimate those two limits precisely. The estimand still lives at $c_0$.

## Smoothness: the assumption that does the work

- **Hahn, Todd and Van der Klaauw (2001)** proved the effect at the cutoff is identified if the conditional expectations of **both** potential outcomes are continuous at $c_0$:
$$
E[Y^0_i \mid X_i = x] \quad\text{and}\quad E[Y^1_i \mid X_i = x] \quad\text{are continuous at } x = c_0 .
$$
<!-- - In words: you could trace both functions through the cutoff **without picking up your pen**. Nothing shifts the outcomes at $c_0$ except the treatment. -->
- This is the RD version of "nature does not jump." The null is continuity; a jump is evidence that *something* happened, and the design's job is to make treatment the only candidate.
<!-- - Weaker than it looks in one way --- no functional form is assumed --- and stronger in another: it must hold for the **unobservable** counterfactual branch on each side. --> 

## Smoothness, in a simulation

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 2.8
set.seed(975)
c0 <- 250; n <- 1200
x  <- runif(n, 150, 350)
y1 <- 100 + 1.25*x + rnorm(n, 0, 15)      # Cunningham's DGP
y0 <-  50 + 0.75*x + rnorm(n, 0, 15)
RED <- "#B2182B"; BLU <- "#2166AC"
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 2.2, 1), cex = 0.8)

plot(x, y1, pch = 16, cex = 0.35, col = adjustcolor(RED, 0.5), ylim = c(80, 500),
     xlab = "running variable", ylab = "outcome", main = "Both potential outcomes")
points(x, y0, pch = 16, cex = 0.35, col = adjustcolor(BLU, 0.5))
abline(v = c0, lty = 2, col = "grey35")
abline(lm(y1 ~ x), col = RED, lwd = 2.2); abline(lm(y0 ~ x), col = BLU, lwd = 2.2)
text(320, 480, expression(E*"["*Y^1*"]"), col = RED, cex = 0.85)
text(330, 235, expression(E*"["*Y^0*"]"), col = BLU, cex = 0.85)

D <- as.integer(x >= c0); y <- ifelse(D == 1, y1, y0)
plot(x, y, pch = 16, cex = 0.35, col = adjustcolor("grey30", 0.5), ylim = c(80, 500),
     xlab = "running variable", ylab = "outcome", main = "What you actually see")
abline(v = c0, lty = 2, col = "grey35")
ml <- lm(y ~ x, subset = D == 0); mr <- lm(y ~ x, subset = D == 1)
xl <- seq(150, c0, 1); xr <- seq(c0, 350, 1)
lines(xl, predict(ml, data.frame(x = xl)), col = BLU, lwd = 2.4)
lines(xr, predict(mr, data.frame(x = xr)), col = RED, lwd = 2.4)
lines(xr, predict(ml, data.frame(x = xr)), col = BLU, lwd = 1.1, lty = 3)
lines(xl, predict(mr, data.frame(x = xl)), col = RED, lwd = 1.1, lty = 3)
a <- predict(ml, data.frame(x = c0)); b <- predict(mr, data.frame(x = c0))
arrows(c0, a, c0, b, code = 3, length = 0.05, lwd = 1.8)
text(c0 + 8, (a + b)/2, expression(tau), adj = 0, cex = 0.95)
```

\vspace{-0.3em}
\footnotesize
$Y^1 = 100 + 1.25X + \varepsilon$ and $Y^0 = 50 + 0.75X + \varepsilon$. Neither jumps at $X = 250$ --- **nothing happens at the cutoff** in the potential outcomes. Apply the switching equation and the *observed* outcome jumps anyway, by exactly the vertical distance between the two functions there. That distance is $\tau$.

## The price of the design

- **You get** an effect that is credible, visible, and hard to fake --- identified by a rule you can read in a statute or a contract.
- **You pay** by learning about one point. If the policy question is "what would this do to everyone?", RD does not answer it.
- The gap between what RD identifies and what a policymaker wants is often large. A study of a drinking age of 21 says nothing about a drinking age of 18.
- **Extrapolating away from the cutoff** requires extra assumptions (Angrist and Rokkanen 2015). Most papers do not, and should say so.
- State the estimand as what it is: *"the average effect for units at the threshold."* Not "the effect." 

# 6.3 Estimation

## Two steps

**Step 1. Recentre the running variable** at the cutoff:
$$
\tilde X_i = X_i - c_0 .
$$
Once centred, the running variable is zero at the cutoff, so the coefficient on $D$ is the jump **there** rather than at $X = 0$.

**Step 2. Regress the outcome on treatment, the running variable, and their interaction:**
$$
Y_i = \alpha + \tau D_i + \beta_1 \tilde X_i + \beta_2\, D_i \cdot \tilde X_i + \varepsilon_i .
$$

- $\beta_1$ is the slope **below** the cutoff, $\beta_1 + \beta_2$ the slope **above**, and $\hat\tau$ estimates the jump.
- The interaction is not optional. It lets the two expected potential-outcome functions have different slopes --- which is to say, it allows heterogeneous treatment effects. Drop it and any difference in trend is loaded onto $\hat\tau$.

## Where the specification comes from

Model each potential outcome as a $p$th-order polynomial in the centred running variable:
$$
E[Y^0 \mid X] = \mu + \beta_{01}\tilde X + \cdots + \beta_{0p}\tilde X^{\,p}, \qquad
E[Y^1 \mid X] = \mu + \tau + \beta_{11}\tilde X + \cdots + \beta_{1p}\tilde X^{\,p}
$$

Apply the **switching equation**, $Y_i = D_i Y^1_i + (1 - D_i)Y^0_i = Y^0_i + D_i(Y^1_i - Y^0_i)$, and take expectations given $X$:
$$
E[Y \mid X] = E[Y^0 \mid X] + D\big(E[Y^1 \mid X] - E[Y^0 \mid X]\big)
$$

which is the regression you actually run:
$$
Y_i = \mu + \beta_{01}\tilde X_i + \cdots + \beta_{0p}\tilde X_i^{\,p}
\;+\; \tau D_i + \gamma_1 D_i \tilde X_i + \cdots + \gamma_p D_i \tilde X_i^{\,p} + \varepsilon_i
$$

- with $\gamma_k = \beta_{1k} - \beta_{0k}$. Interacting $D$ with **every** polynomial term is what lets the two sides take genuinely different shapes.
- The treatment effect **at the cutoff** is $\tau$. 

## Get the shape wrong and the answer is nonsense

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 2.85
set.seed(1234)
n <- 4000; c0 <- 250
x  <- rnorm(n, 250, 30); xc <- x - c0; D <- as.integer(x >= c0)
y  <- 1000 + 0.75*xc - 0.5*xc^2 + 1.5*xc^3 + rnorm(n, 0, 1000)   # TRUE EFFECT IS ZERO
RED <- "#B2182B"; BLU <- "#2166AC"
w  <- c(190, 310)                                   # zoom: the cubic tails are off-scale
b  <- seq(w[1], w[2], length.out = 31); mid <- head(b, -1) + diff(b)/2
k  <- x >= w[1] & x <= w[2]
bm <- tapply(y[k], cut(x[k], b), mean)
tau <- numeric(3)                                   # kept for the table on the next slide
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 2.2, 1), cex = 0.8)
for (deg in 1:3) {
  lim <- numeric(2)
  if (deg != 2) {
    plot(mid, bm, pch = 16, cex = 0.6, col = "grey45", xlim = w,
         xlab = "running variable", ylab = "outcome",
         main = if (deg == 1) "Linear fit (underfit)" else "Cubic fit (correct)")
    abline(v = c0, lty = 2, col = "grey45")
  }
  for (s in 0:1) {
    dk <- data.frame(x = x[D == s], y = y[D == s])  # fitted on ALL the data, not the window
    m  <- lm(y ~ poly(x, deg, raw = TRUE), data = dk)
    lim[s + 1] <- predict(m, data.frame(x = c0))
    if (deg != 2) {
      xx <- seq(if (s == 0) w[1] else c0, if (s == 0) c0 else w[2], length.out = 200)
      lines(xx, predict(m, data.frame(x = xx)), col = if (s == 0) BLU else RED, lwd = 2.3)
    }
  }
  tau[deg] <- lim[2] - lim[1]
  if (deg != 2) {
    arrows(c0, lim[1], c0, lim[2], code = 3, length = 0.05, lwd = 1.8)
    text(c0 + 8, mean(lim), paste0(if (tau[deg] > 0) "+" else "-",
         formatC(abs(tau[deg]), format = "d", big.mark = ",")), adj = 0, cex = 0.85, font = 2)
  }
}
```

\vspace{-0.3em}
\footnotesize
The truth is a **cubic** in the running variable and the treatment effect is exactly **zero** --- the two potential outcomes are identical, so they touch everywhere. Straight lines cannot bend where the data bend, so they arrive at the cutoff at the wrong heights and manufacture a jump out of nothing.

## The damage, quantified

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
cat("\\begin{center}\\small\n\\begin{tabular}{lrrr}\n\\toprule\n")
cat("Fitted polynomial & $X$ & $X, X^2$ & $X, X^2, X^3$ \\\\\n\\midrule\n")
cat(sprintf("$\\hat\\tau$ & $%s$ & $%s$ & $%s$ \\\\\n",
    formatC(tau[1], format = "d", big.mark = ","),
    formatC(tau[2], format = "d", big.mark = ","),
    formatC(tau[3], format = "d", big.mark = ",")))
cat("\\bottomrule\n\\end{tabular}\n\\end{center}\n")
```


- **The true effect is zero.** Underfit by two orders and you get about $-170{,}000$; by one, about $+59{,}000$. Get the order right and the estimate collapses into noise.
- These are not merely biased --- they are wrong by *five orders of magnitude*, and they would be reported as **highly statistically significant**.
- The mechanism is the extrapolation. $\hat\tau$ is the gap between two fitted values **at a boundary**, and boundary predictions are exactly where a misspecified polynomial errs most.

## But do not solve it with more polynomials

- The obvious fix --- keep raising $p$ --- is the wrong one. **Gelman and Imbens (2019)** give three reasons not to go above quadratic:
  1. High-order polynomials put **large, erratic weights** on observations far from the cutoff, so distant data drive an estimate that is supposed to be local.
  2. Estimates are **highly sensitive** to the order chosen, with no principled way to pick it.
  3. The resulting confidence intervals have **poor coverage**.
- Their recommendation, now standard: **local linear or local quadratic**, fitted only near the cutoff.
<!-- - Note that underfitting is a threat too --- that is what the last slide showed. Both directions produce spurious estimates.-->
- Which reframes the problem. Instead of "what shape fits the whole range?", ask "how small a neighbourhood can I afford, and fit a line inside it." 

## The boundary problem with "rectangular kernel"

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 1.75
c0 <- 5
RED <- "#B2182B"; BLU <- "#2166AC"
f0 <- function(x) 2 + 0.55*x
f1 <- function(x) f0(x) + 2.4
par(mar = c(3.4, 3.5, 0.6, 0.8), mgp = c(2.1, 0.7, 0), cex = 0.7)
plot(NULL, xlim = c(1.6, 8.6), ylim = c(2.4, 10.2),
     xlab = "running variable", ylab = "outcome")
abline(v = c(3, 7), col = "grey86"); abline(v = c0, lty = 2, col = "grey30")
xs <- seq(1.6, 8.6, 0.02)
lines(xs, f0(xs), col = BLU, lwd = 2); lines(xs, f1(xs), col = RED, lwd = 2)
## a bin mean sits at the bin CENTRE, so it hits the boundary at the wrong height
segments(3, f0(4), 5, f0(4), col = BLU, lwd = 3)
segments(5, f1(6), 7, f1(6), col = RED, lwd = 3)
points(c0, f0(c0), pch = 16, cex = 1.2); points(c0, f1(c0), pch = 16, cex = 1.2)
points(c0, f0(4), pch = 21, bg = "white", col = BLU, cex = 1.3, lwd = 2)
points(c0, f1(6), pch = 21, bg = "white", col = RED, cex = 1.3, lwd = 2)
text(c0 + 0.13, f0(c0) + 0.30, "A", adj = 0, cex = 0.95, font = 2)
text(c0 + 0.13, f1(c0) - 0.32, "B", adj = 0, cex = 0.95, font = 2)
text(c0 - 0.13, f0(4) - 0.32, "A'", adj = 1, cex = 0.95, col = BLU)
text(c0 - 0.13, f1(6) + 0.30, "B'", adj = 1, cex = 0.95, col = RED)
arrows(4.15, f0(c0), 4.15, f1(c0), code = 3, length = 0.05, lwd = 1.6)
text(4.03, (f0(c0) + f1(c0))/2, "true", adj = 1, cex = 0.8)
arrows(5.85, f0(4), 5.85, f1(6), code = 3, length = 0.05, lwd = 1.6, col = "grey25")
text(5.85, f0(4) - 0.6, "from the bins", adj = 0.5, cex = 0.8, col = "grey25")
```

\vspace{-0.4em}
\footnotesize
The true effect is $\overline{AB} = 2.4$. But a bin mean sits at the bin's **centre**, not at its edge, so the left limit is read off at $A'$ and the right at $B'$: the estimate is $\overline{A'B'} = 3.5$, too large by $46\%$. **The trends cause the bias** --- flatten the two lines and $A' \to A$, $B' \to B$. 
<!-- It is a property of the estimator, not of noise, so it does not shrink with sample size.-->

## Kernel and bandwidth

- The standard fix (Hahn, Todd and Van der Klaauw): fit a **line** inside the window rather than a mean, and let it extrapolate the short distance to the boundary. That is local linear regression, and it substantially reduces the bias.

$$
(\hat a, \hat b) \;=\; \arg\min_{a, b} \sum_{i=1}^n \big(Y_i - a - b(X_i - c_0)\big)^2\,
K\!\left(\frac{X_i - c_0}{h}\right) \mathbf{1}\{X_i > c_0\}
$$

- Think of kernel regression as a weighted regression restricted to a window. Two distinct choices, often confused:
  - The **kernel** $K(\cdot)$ is the *shape* of the window --- how weight declines with distance from the cutoff.
  - The **bandwidth** $h$ is the *width* of the window --- how far from the cutoff you are willing to look.
- Averaging within a bin **is** a rectangular kernel: equal weight to every unit inside. That is exactly the biased case above.

## Three choices: $h$, $K(\cdot)$, and $p$

- **The bandwidth $h$.** Smaller: fewer observations, less bias, more variance. Larger: more data, less variance, more bias if the included units depart from the true function. This choice matters most.
- **The kernel $K(\cdot)$.**
  - *Rectangular*: equal weight inside the window, zero outside --- a plain window.
  - *Triangular*: weight declines linearly to zero at the edge.
  - *Epanechnikov*: parabolic weighting.
- **The polynomial order $p$.** $p = 0$ is a difference in means --- intuitive, but it *is* the boundary problem. $p > 1$ addresses it but risks overfitting and instability. **Local linear ($p = 1$) is generally preferred.**
- Calonico, Cattaneo and Titiunik (2014) recommend the **triangular kernel with an MSE-optimal bandwidth**: maximum weight at the cutoff, zero at the window's edge.
- There is no universally correct answer. Report what you chose, and show the answer does not turn on it.

## The three kernels, written out

Let $u = (X_i - c_0)/h$, so that $|u| \leq 1$ means "inside the window".

\vspace{-0.3em}
\begin{center}
\small
\begin{tabular}{ll}
\toprule
Rectangular (uniform) & $K(u) = \tfrac{1}{2}\,\mathbf{1}\{|u| \leq 1\}$ \\
Triangular            & $K(u) = (1 - |u|)\,\mathbf{1}\{|u| \leq 1\}$ \\
Epanechnikov          & $K(u) = \tfrac{3}{4}(1 - u^2)\,\mathbf{1}\{|u| \leq 1\}$ \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 1.15
u <- seq(-1.6, 1.6, 0.002)
ins <- abs(u) <= 1
kr <- ifelse(ins, 0.5, 0)
kt <- ifelse(ins, 1 - abs(u), 0)
ke <- ifelse(ins, 0.75*(1 - u^2), 0)
RED <- "#B2182B"; BLU <- "#2166AC"
par(mar = c(3.2, 3.4, 0.5, 0.8), mgp = c(1.9, 0.6, 0), cex = 0.65)
plot(NULL, xlim = c(-1.6, 1.6), ylim = c(0, 1.08), xlab = "u = (X - c0)/h",
     ylab = "K(u)")
abline(v = 0, lty = 2, col = "grey60"); abline(h = 0, col = "grey80")
lines(u, kr, col = "grey35", lwd = 2.4)
lines(u, kt, col = RED,     lwd = 2.4)
lines(u, ke, col = BLU,     lwd = 2.4)
legend("topright", c("rectangular", "triangular", "Epanechnikov"),
       col = c("grey35", RED, BLU), lwd = 2.4, bty = "n", cex = 0.9, seg.len = 1.4)
```

\vspace{-0.4em}
\footnotesize

- All three have **compact support** --- $K(u) = 0$ once $|u| > 1$.
- The constants $\tfrac12$ and $\tfrac34$ make each integrate to one, and are **irrelevant here**: scaling every weight equally leaves the WLS solution unchanged.
<!-- - **Why triangular is the default.** It is MSE-optimal for estimating a regression function *at a boundary point* (Cheng, Fan and Marron 1997) --- which is exactly the RD problem. -->

## The recipe

1. Choose a polynomial order $p$ and a kernel $K(\cdot)$.
2. Select a bandwidth $h$.
3. **Above the cutoff**, run weighted least squares of $Y$ on a constant and $p$ terms in $(X_i - c_0)$, with weights $K((X_i - c_0)/h)$. The intercept estimates $\mu_+ = \lim_{x \downarrow c_0} E[Y \mid X = x]$:
$$
\hat Y_i = \hat\mu_+ + \hat\mu_{+,1}(X_i - c_0) + \cdots + \hat\mu_{+,p}(X_i - c_0)^p
$$
4. **Repeat below the cutoff** for $\hat\mu_-$.
5. The sharp RD point estimate is the difference of the two intercepts:
$$
\hat\tau = \hat\mu_+ - \hat\mu_- .
$$

- In practice this is one line: `rdrobust(y, x, c = 0)` in R, `rdrobust y x, c(0)` in Stata.

## What "weighted least squares" means in step 3

Give unit $i$ the weight $w_i = K\!\big((X_i - c_0)/h\big)$ and minimise the **weighted** sum of squares:
$$
\hat\beta \;=\; \arg\min_{\beta} \sum_{i=1}^{n} w_i \big(Y_i - x_i'\beta\big)^2 ,
\qquad x_i = \big(1,\; \tilde X_i,\; \tilde X_i^2, \ldots, \tilde X_i^{\,p}\big)', \quad \tilde X_i = X_i - c_0
$$
with the closed form $\;\hat\beta = (X'WX)^{-1}X'WY$, where $W = \operatorname{diag}(w_1, \ldots, w_n)$.

<!-- - **The intercept is the answer.** At the cutoff $\tilde X = 0$, so $x = (1, 0, \ldots, 0)'$ and $\hat\mu_+ = \hat\beta_1$. Recentring means the boundary prediction *is* a coefficient --- there is no separate extrapolation step. -->
- Units with $|\tilde X_i| > h$ get $w_i = 0$ and contribute nothing to either $X'WX$ or $X'WY$.
- **Rectangular kernel $\Rightarrow$ plain OLS on the subsample**, because every in-window weight is then equal. 

<!-- 
## These are not the weights from your econometrics course

- In the standard treatment, WLS is a **GLS** device: with heteroskedastic errors $\mathrm{Var}(\varepsilon_i) = \sigma_i^2$, setting $w_i \propto 1/\sigma_i^2$ delivers the *efficient* estimator. The weights are chosen to buy **precision**.
- Here the weights are a function of $X_i$ alone --- they know nothing about $\sigma_i^2$ --- and they buy **locality** instead. We downweight distant, informative observations *on purpose*, to cut bias.
- So this estimator is **inefficient by construction**, and that is the point: the whole apparatus of §6.3 is spending variance to buy bias reduction near the boundary.
- Two consequences worth stating:
  1. The weights do **not** correct heteroskedasticity. You still need heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors --- and, from the earlier slide, you still must not cluster on the running variable.
  2. Reported sample sizes are misleading. `rdrobust` prints an *effective* $N$ for this reason: with a triangular kernel, a unit at the edge of the window counts for almost nothing. \hfill \emph{(added)}
-->

## Choosing the bandwidth

Bias grows with $h$, variance falls with it. Writing each as a function of $h$ and minimising:
$$
\mathrm{MSE}(h) \;\approx\; \underbrace{B^2 h^{2(p+1)}}_{\text{bias}^2} + \underbrace{\frac{V}{nh}}_{\text{variance}}
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
h_{MSE} \;\propto\; \underbrace{V^{\frac{1}{2p+3}}}_{\text{noise}}\;
\underbrace{B^{-\frac{2}{2p+3}}}_{\text{curvature}}\;
\underbrace{n^{-\frac{1}{2p+3}}}_{\text{sample size}}
$$



- **Noise $V$: positive exponent.** Noisier data $\Rightarrow$ a **wider** window, to average the noise away. If $V \to 0$, then $h \to 0$ --- use only points at the cutoff.\footnote{*The Remix* states the $n$ and noise directions the other way round. }
- **Curvature $B$: negative.** More curvature $\Rightarrow$ a **narrower** window. If $B \to 0$ (a truly linear CEF), $h \to \infty$ --- just run OLS on everything.
- **Sample size $n$: negative.** More data $\Rightarrow$ a **narrower** window. The extra data buys *less bias*, not a wider window --- though the count inside it, $nh \propto n^{(2p+2)/(2p+3)}$, still grows.
- Imbens and Kalyanaraman (2012) gave the first data-driven rule; Calonico, Cattaneo and Titiunik (2014) is the standard. Bandwidths may differ by side.


## Why the obvious confidence interval is wrong

- The local polynomial is a **nonparametric approximation** to an unknown function. It does not fit perfectly inside the window, so $\hat\tau$ carries an approximation bias $B$ as well as sampling noise. Honest inference needs
$$
CI = \big[(\hat\tau - B) \pm 1.96 \sqrt{V}\big].
$$
- The conventional interval, $CI_{us} = [\hat\tau \pm 1.96\sqrt{\hat V}]$, simply **assumes $B = 0$** --- it centres the interval on a biased point estimate.
- The consequence is **over-rejection** of the null of no effect. Cattaneo, Jansson and Ma discourage reporting these, and they are not credible under even moderate bias.
- Worse, there is an internal contradiction: the MSE-optimal bandwidth is chosen *to trade bias against variance*, so at that bandwidth the bias is deliberately **not** negligible.

## Three intervals

\begin{center}
\small
\begin{tabular}{lccl}
\toprule
Interval & Centred at & Standard error & Verdict \\
\midrule
Conventional, $CI_{us}$        & $\hat\tau$          & $\sqrt{\hat V}$      & do not use \\
Bias-corrected, $CI_{bc}$      & $\hat\tau - \hat B$ & $\sqrt{\hat V}$      & better, but ignores noise in $\hat B$ \\
Robust bias-corrected, $CI_{rbc}$ & $\hat\tau - \hat B$ & $\sqrt{\hat V_{bc}}$ & \textbf{report this} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

- Bias correction subtracts an estimate of $B$. But $\hat B$ is itself estimated, and pretending otherwise distorts coverage in finite samples.
- **Robust** bias correction folds the variability of $\hat B$ into the variance term. Intervals get somewhat wider for the same bandwidth --- that is the honest price of the correction.
- This is what `rdrobust` reports by default. Report the robust row, and say that you did.

## Do not take my word for it: a coverage experiment

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 2.7
RED <- "#B2182B"; BLU <- "#2166AC"; GRN <- "#1B7837"
hs   <- c(0.06,0.08,0.10,0.13,0.16,0.20,0.25,0.30,0.40,0.50)
conv <- c(93.8,93.2,92.3,93.7,92.3,89.2,73.7,48.0, 1.7, 0.0)
bc   <- c(81.3,76.8,80.2,80.8,82.3,80.3,84.3,80.2,83.2,81.8)
rbc  <- c(92.8,90.7,92.5,93.3,95.3,94.8,96.8,95.0,96.2,94.8)
par(mar = c(4, 4.2, 1.2, 1), cex = 0.8)
plot(hs, conv, type = "n", ylim = c(0, 100), xlab = "bandwidth  h",
     ylab = "coverage of a nominal 95% CI (%)")
abline(h = 95, lty = 2, col = "grey45"); abline(v = 0.19, lty = 3, col = "grey65")
text(0.197, 10, "MSE-optimal h", adj = 0, cex = 0.65, col = "grey40", srt = 90)
lines(hs, conv, col = RED, lwd = 2.4); points(hs, conv, pch = 16, col = RED, cex = 0.7)
lines(hs, bc,  col = BLU, lwd = 2.4, lty = 5); points(hs, bc, pch = 17, col = BLU, cex = 0.7)
lines(hs, rbc, col = GRN, lwd = 2.4); points(hs, rbc, pch = 15, col = GRN, cex = 0.7)
text(0.505,  5, "Conventional", col = RED, adj = 1, cex = 0.75)
text(0.505, 74, "Bias-corrected", col = BLU, adj = 1, cex = 0.75)
text(0.505, 99, "Robust bias-corrected", col = GRN, adj = 1, cex = 0.75)
```

\vspace{-0.4em}
\footnotesize
$2{,}000$ simulated samples per bandwidth, $n = 2{,}000$, known $\tau = 0.20$, a curved $E[Y|X]$ on both sides. For each sample we build all three intervals and ask a single question: **does it contain the true $\tau$?** A 95\% interval should say yes 95\% of the time.

## Read that figure slowly

- **Conventional (red).** Fine when $h$ is small, because then bias is genuinely negligible. It then falls off a cliff: $74\%$ at $h=0.25$, $48\%$ at $h=0.30$, and **$0\%$ at $h=0.50$**. A "95\% interval" that never covers the truth. Nothing warns you --- the output looks completely normal.
- **Bias-corrected (blue).** Flat at about $81\%$ *everywhere*. Recentring fixed the location but the interval is still too short, because $\hat B$ is itself noisy and this interval pretends it is not.
- **Robust bias-corrected (green).** Flat at roughly $95\%$ across an eightfold range of bandwidths. That flatness *is* the property you are buying.
- The lesson is not "conventional intervals are a bit optimistic." It is that their failure is **invisible and unbounded**, and it grows precisely as you widen the window to buy precision.

\footnotesize
*Teaching note: run it live with two bandwidths --- $h = 0.10$ and $h = 0.40$ --- and let the class predict before you reveal.*

## A short detour: what clustering a standard error does

- OLS standard errors assume the errors $\varepsilon_i$ are **independent across observations**. Each observation is a fresh piece of information.
- Suppose instead the data arrive in **groups**, and everyone in a group shares a common shock: students in a classroom share a teacher, firms in an industry share a shock. Then residuals inside a group move together.
- Independent draws are being double-counted. Your **effective** sample size is closer to the *number of groups* than to the number of observations, and conventional standard errors are too small.
- A **cluster-robust** standard error allows arbitrary correlation *within* each group while assuming independence *across* groups. It normally makes standard errors **larger**.
- The fine print, which is the whole story today: the formula's justification is asymptotic **in the number of clusters $G$**. With few clusters it is unreliable, and there is no warning message.

\footnotesize
*We return to clustering properly in the panel-data lecture. Today you need only the idea: a cluster is a set of observations that share something, and the fix needs many such sets.*

## Why RD researchers clustered on the running variable

- **The problem it was meant to solve.** Most running variables are not continuous but **multi-valued**: BAC to $0.001$, test scores in whole points, age in months. Many observations share each value --- call these **mass points**.
- With mass points you cannot literally take a limit at $c_0$. You fit a polynomial across the mass points instead, and that polynomial will not pass exactly through $E[Y \mid X = x]$ at every one of them. The gap is **specification error**.
- **Lee and Card's (2008) insight:** every observation sitting at the same mass point shares *exactly the same* specification error. That is precisely the structure of a group shock.
- So they proposed treating **each distinct value of the running variable as one cluster.** That is the answer to "clustering at what level?" --- not individuals, not counties, not years. One cluster per unique value of $X$.
  - In Hansen's data: one cluster per BAC reading. In a test-score RD: one cluster per integer score.
- The logic is genuinely clever, the recommendation spread through most subsequent RD papers, and it is now understood to be **wrong**.

## Why it fails --- and it fails in a surprising direction

\begin{center}
\small
\begin{tabular}{lrrrrr}
\toprule
Bandwidth $h$ & $N$ & Clusters $G$ & Robust SE & Clustered SE & Ratio \\
\midrule
$0.050$ (Hansen's) & $90{,}074$ & $101$ & $0.00450$ & $0.00333$ & $0.74$ \\
$0.020$            & $38{,}349$ & $41$  & $0.00657$ & $0.00421$ & $0.64$ \\
$0.010$            & $20{,}154$ & $21$  & $0.00911$ & $0.00476$ & $\mathbf{0.52}$ \\
$0.005$            & $10{,}567$ & $11$  & $0.01303$ & $0.00740$ & $0.57$ \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

\vspace{-0.2em}

- Hansen's recidivism regression, clustered on the distinct BAC readings. **Clustering makes the standard error *smaller* --- by up to half.** Every instinct you just built says it should get bigger.
- Smaller standard errors mean larger $t$-statistics and **more rejections of a true null**. That is Kolesár and Rothe's inflated Type I error, in one column.
- Two things are going wrong. First, look at $G$: shrinking the bandwidth to reduce bias destroys clusters. At $h = 0.005$ there are $20{,}000$ observations but **$11$ clusters**. The formula's asymptotics are nowhere in sight.
- Second, and deeper: specification error is a **fixed function of $x$**, not a random draw. It does not average out over repeated samples, because it is the same every time. Clustering prices a randomness that is not there.

## What to do instead

- **Use heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors** --- what `rdrobust` reports by default. They do not pretend to solve the approximation problem, which is the honest position.
- **Or use honest confidence intervals** (`RDHonest`, Armstrong--Kolesár). You state a bound on the curvature of $E[Y|X]$ and the interval is guaranteed to cover at the stated rate given that bound. The assumption is explicit rather than buried.
- **Sparse data near the cutoff** is the recurring practical problem. When observations are thin, or the running variable is coarse, even robust intervals may fail to centre properly.
- **Randomization inference** (Cattaneo, Jansson and Ma; `rdlocrand`): assume that within a **small window** around the cutoff treatment is effectively randomly assigned, then analyse that window as an experiment. Weaker assumptions than local polynomials, and better behaved when data are sparse.
- **Reading an older RD paper** that clusters on the running variable? That is not fraud --- it was the recommended practice. Ask whether the result survives robust standard errors.

# 6.4 Challenges to Identification

## Five ways continuity fails

Continuity is the whole design. It breaks when:

1. The **assignment rule is known** in advance;
2. Agents are **interested** in adjusting their score;
3. Agents **have time** to adjust;
4. The **cutoff is endogenous** --- something else changes at $c_0$ too;
5. There is **nonrandom heaping** along the running variable.

\vspace{0.3em}

- Conditions 1--3 together are the recipe for **sorting**: retaking an exam, reporting income just below a threshold, delaying a birth. All three are needed --- an agent with an incentive *and* an opportunity.
- Condition 4 is different, and often overlooked. Turning 18 brings adult criminal penalties --- and also voting rights, high-school graduation, and much else. The cutoff is real but not clean.
- Condition 5 is gets its own treatment below.

## Sorting, and the two rooms

- Two rooms of patients. Room A gets the life-saving treatment; room B gets nothing. If you are in room B, you walk across the hall --- unless crossing is impossible.
- If everyone crosses, A is crowded and B is empty. That imbalance is the **observable footprint** of sorting: motives are invisible, but headcounts are not.
- Formally: with a desirable treatment assigned by $X \geq c_0$, agents who *can* choose $X$ just above $c_0$. If that ability correlates with potential outcomes, the comparison at the cutoff is contaminated.
- Behavioural theory yields a **testable prediction**: a discontinuity in the *density* of the running variable. 


## The McCrary density test

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 2.5
RED <- "#B2182B"
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 2.2, 1), cex = 0.8)
xs <- seq(-1, 1, 0.002); c0 <- 0
f  <- function(x) dnorm(x, 0, 0.45)
plot(xs, f(xs), type = "n", xlab = "running variable", ylab = "density",
     main = "No manipulation", ylim = c(0, 1.55))
lines(xs[xs <  c0], f(xs[xs <  c0]), lwd = 2.4, col = "grey25")
lines(xs[xs >= c0], f(xs[xs >= c0]), lwd = 2.4, col = "grey25")
abline(v = c0, lty = 2, col = RED)
text(0.07, 1.42, "continuous through the cutoff", adj = 0, cex = 0.68, col = "grey30")

g <- function(x) ifelse(x < c0, f(x)*0.72, f(x)*1.28)
plot(xs, g(xs), type = "n", xlab = "running variable", ylab = "density",
     main = "Manipulation", ylim = c(0, 1.55))
lines(xs[xs <  c0], g(xs[xs <  c0]), lwd = 2.4, col = "grey25")
lines(xs[xs >= c0], g(xs[xs >= c0]), lwd = 2.4, col = "grey25")
abline(v = c0, lty = 2, col = RED)
arrows(0, g(-1e-6), 0, g(1e-6), code = 3, length = 0.04, lwd = 1.6, col = RED)
text(0.07, 1.42, "room B emptied into room A", adj = 0, cex = 0.68, col = "grey30")
```

\vspace{-0.4em}

- Under the null of no manipulation the density of $X$ is **continuous** at $c_0$; under the alternative it bunches on the treated side.
- Mechanically: partition the running variable into bins, count observations per bin, treat the counts as an outcome, fit a local linear regression on each side, and test whether the limits agree.
- Use `rddensity` (Cattaneo, Jansson and Ma) --- local polynomials with less bias at the border than the original. **It needs a lot of data at $c_0$** to separate a real jump from noise.

## Running the test: `rddensity` on real data

```r
library(rddensity)
dwi <- read.csv("data/hansen_dwi.csv")
bac <- dwi$bac1[dwi$bac1 > 0]

out <- rddensity(bac, c = 0.08)     # X and the cutoff. That is the whole call.
summary(out)                        # T = -0.14, p = 0.89

rdplotdensity(out, bac)             # the picture that belongs in the paper
```

\vspace{-0.3em}

- The call takes the **running variable only** --- no outcome, no covariates. You are testing the distribution of $X$, nothing else.
- What to read in the output: the **robust bias-corrected** $T$ statistic and its $p$-value. Same three-interval logic as before; `rddensity` is running a local polynomial too.
- On Hansen's stops: $T = -0.14$, $p = 0.89$. **Fail to reject.** The sign is negative --- marginally *fewer* stops just above $0.08$ --- the opposite of what sorting would produce.
- Always run `rdplotdensity` as well. The test is one number; manipulation is a shape.

## Making the test fail, on purpose

```r
# sabotage: a fraction of drivers just below 0.08 talk their way out of a reading
zone <- which(bac >= 0.078 & bac < 0.080)           # 2,786 stops
drop <- sample(zone, floor(0.20 * length(zone)))
rddensity(bac[-drop], c = 0.08)
```

\begin{center}
\small
\begin{tabular}{lrrrl}
\toprule
Data & Stops deleted & $T$ & $p$ & Verdict \\
\midrule
Hansen's actual stops   & ---     & $-0.14$ & $0.89$    & no evidence \\
Delete 10\% just below  & $278$   & $2.25$  & $0.025$   & rejects, barely \\
Delete 20\% just below  & $557$   & $4.69$  & $<0.0001$ & rejects decisively \\
Delete 40\% just below  & $1{,}114$ & $9.35$ & $<0.0001$ & overwhelming \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

\vspace{-0.2em}

- **Worth ten minutes of class.** A test students only ever see *pass* teaches nothing about what it detects. Break the data yourself and it becomes legible.
- Read the table as a **power curve**: with $213{,}000$ stops, deleting $10\%$ of a narrow strip sits at the edge of detection and $20\%$ is caught easily. At a tenth the sample, none of it would be.
- **The real lesson.** "The density test passed" means little without knowing what it *could* have detected --- Almond et al. passed it too. Set a placebo cutoff at $0.10$ as a second exercise.

## Covariate balance and placebo cutoffs

- **Covariate balance.** Pre-treatment characteristics cannot be caused by treatment, so they must not jump at $c_0$. Run the same RD with each covariate as the outcome and find nothing. 
- A jump in a covariate is serious. It means something *other than* treatment changes at the cutoff --- and if an observed characteristic jumps, unobserved ones probably do too.
- **Placebo cutoffs.** Imbens and Lemieux (2008): take one side of the discontinuity, use the median of the running variable there as a fake cutoff $c_0'$, and test for a jump in the outcome. You do not want to find anything.
- The identifying assumptions cannot be tested directly. What these do is supply **indirect evidence** that may be persuasive --- placebo logic, looking where there should be no effect.

## Nonrandom heaping: a design that passed its tests

- **Almond, Doyle, Kowalski and Williams (2010)** wanted the returns to medical care --- hard, because doctors assign care by expected outcome, which is selection bias by construction. The Perfect Doctor problem again.
- Their insight: babies below $1{,}500$g are classified **"very low birth weight"** and receive heightened attention. Birth weight is the running variable, $1{,}500$g the cutoff, and the rule is written down.
- Using hospital records linked to mortality, they found one-year mortality about **one percentage point lower** just below the threshold, against a mean of $5.5\%$. A large effect, and one that appeared to far exceed the cost of the care.
- They ran the **McCrary test at $1{,}500$g and found nothing.** Density continuous, no evidence of manipulation. Satisfied, they proceeded.
- Everything about this is the textbook procedure, done competently. Hold that thought.

## Then look at the whole distribution

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 2.75
set.seed(975)
RED <- "#B2182B"; BLU <- "#2166AC"
n  <- 900000
bw <- c(rnorm(n*0.88, 3350, 470), rnorm(n*0.12, 2250, 640))
bw <- bw[bw > 700 & bw < 4600]
u  <- runif(length(bw)); oz <- 28.349523
bw[u < 0.18] <- round(bw[u < 0.18]/100)*100              # recorded to the nearest 100 g
kk <- u >= 0.18 & u < 0.32
bw[kk] <- round(bw[kk]/oz)*oz                            # recorded in whole ounces
gg <- round(bw)
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4.2, 2.0, 1), cex = 0.8)
drawpanel <- function(lo, hi, main, labx, laby) {
  tb <- table(gg[gg >= lo & gg <= hi])
  xs <- as.numeric(names(tb)); ys <- as.integer(tb)
  plot(xs, ys, type = "n", xlab = "birth weight (grams)", ylab = "number of births",
       main = main, xlim = c(lo, hi))
  abline(v = 1500, col = BLU, lwd = 2.2, lty = 2)
  points(xs, ys, type = "h", col = "grey62", lwd = 1)
  points(xs[xs %% 100 == 0], ys[xs %% 100 == 0], type = "h", col = RED, lwd = 1.8)
  text(labx, max(ys)*laby, "VLBW cutoff", col = BLU, adj = 0, cex = 0.7)
}
drawpanel(1000, 3000, "The whole distribution", 1540, 0.55)
legend("topleft", legend = c("multiples of 100g", "all other weights"),
       col = c(RED, "grey62"), lwd = c(1.8, 1), bty = "n", cex = 0.66)
drawpanel(1350, 1650, "Zoomed on the cutoff", 1508, 0.86)
```

\vspace{-0.4em}
\footnotesize
**Barreca, Guldi, Lindo and Waddell** looked at the *shape* of the whole distribution rather than at one point in it, and found **heaping**: excess mass at every round $100$g mark, and at whole-ounce values, from hospitals rounding. Nature does not produce piles of babies every hundred grams. Heaping is either rounding or manipulation. *(Stylised reproduction.)*

## Why heaping fakes an effect at *every* cutoff

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 3.1
set.seed(975)
RED <- "#B2182B"; BLU <- "#2166AC"
mort <- function(x) 0.085 - 0.000035*(x - 1300)
panel <- function(c0, main, h = 80) {
  xs <- seq(c0-h, c0+h, 5)
  is_heap <- xs %% 100 == 0                       # exactly one heap inside the window
  y <- mort(xs) + ifelse(is_heap, 0.020, 0) + rnorm(length(xs), 0, 0.0016)
  plot(xs, y, type = "n", xlab = "birth weight (grams)", ylab = "one-year mortality",
       main = main, ylim = c(0.068, 0.108), xlim = c(c0-h, c0+h))
  abline(v = c0, lty = 2, col = "grey35")
  points(xs[!is_heap], y[!is_heap], pch = 16, cex = 0.8, col = adjustcolor("grey30", 0.75))
  L <- xs < c0; R <- xs >= c0
  ml <- lm(y[L] ~ xs[L]); mr <- lm(y[R] ~ xs[R])
  xl <- seq(c0-h, c0, 1); xr <- seq(c0, c0+h, 1)
  lines(xl, coef(ml)[1] + coef(ml)[2]*xl, col = BLU, lwd = 2.6)
  lines(xr, coef(mr)[1] + coef(mr)[2]*xr, col = RED, lwd = 2.6)
  points(xs[is_heap], y[is_heap], pch = 17, cex = 1.5, col = RED)
  a <- coef(ml)[1] + coef(ml)[2]*c0; b <- coef(mr)[1] + coef(mr)[2]*c0
  arrows(c0, a, c0, b, code = 3, length = 0.045, lwd = 2)
  text(c0 - 9, (a+b)/2 + 0.013, sprintf("%.1f pp \"benefit\"", 100*(b-a)), adj = 1, cex = 0.7)
  text(c0 + 4, y[is_heap] + 0.004, sprintf("heap at %d", c0), col = RED, adj = 0, cex = 0.68)
}
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4.4, 2.0, 1), cex = 0.8)
panel(1500, "Cutoff 1,500g  (the real rule)")
legend("bottomleft", legend = c("heaped birth weights", "all other weights"),
       pch = c(17, 16), col = c(RED, "grey30"), bty = "n", cex = 0.66)
panel(1600, "Cutoff 1,600g  (a pure placebo)")
```

\vspace{-0.4em}
\footnotesize
The window is narrow enough that **one** heap falls inside it, and it sits on the $\geq c_0$ side --- the control side. That single pile of frail babies lifts the right-hand limit, so being *below* the cutoff looks protective. The right panel runs the identical exercise at $1{,}600$g, where **nothing happens to anyone**.

## Unpacking that figure --- the composition effect

- **Step 1. Heaped babies are different babies.** Rounding is not random --- it happens in rushed deliveries and less-equipped hospitals. Barreca et al. show heaped births have less-educated mothers, less prenatal care, and **higher mortality** than their unheaped neighbours.
- **Step 2. Which side of the rule does the heap fall on?** VLBW means $< 1{,}500$g, so a baby recorded at *exactly* $1{,}500$g is **not** treated. The whole heap sits in the **control** group, at the boundary.
- **Step 3. That drags the control limit up.** The right-hand limit is computed from data beginning with a pile of unusually frail babies, so it is biased upward. Subtracting an inflated control mean makes being *below* the cutoff look protective.
- **Step 4. Step 3 never used the number $1{,}500$.** It needs only "*a heap sits at the cutoff*." So the same apparent benefit appears at **any** $100$g mark from $1{,}000$ to $3{,}000$g --- the right panel above.
- **Step 5. Conclude.** Nothing changes at $1{,}600$g, and no effect can be present at twenty placebo cutoffs. What jumps is not the care these babies receive but **who is recorded there**: composition, not treatment.

## What passing the density test does *not* prove

- The McCrary test asks exactly one question --- *is the density continuous at $c_0$?* --- and at $1{,}500$g the honest answer was **yes**. Heaping does not make the density jump; it makes it **spiky**, and a spike sitting *on* the cutoff is not a step *across* it.
- The problem lived in a different feature of the same distribution. The test was not wrong. It was answering a different question from the one that mattered.
- **The general lesson.** A test on one feature cannot clear a problem living in another. In the matching lecture, means passed while variances failed. Here, the density passed while the composition failed.
- **Plot the raw distribution.** Every time. A histogram would have shown this in five seconds; the test statistic never would.
- Barreca et al.'s remedy --- drop the suspect observations and re-estimate --- is the **donut hole**, next.

## The donut-hole RD

- If units *at* the cutoff are suspect --- heaped, rounded, or manipulated --- but units nearby are fine, drop the suspect ones and re-estimate. That is the **donut hole**.
- The justification is clean: RD compares means *as we approach* the threshold, so the estimate should not be sensitive to observations exactly at it.
- In Almond et al.'s data, dropping about **$2\%$** of observations cut the estimated one-year mortality effect roughly **in half**.
- The costs are real:
  - You lose observations you often cannot afford to lose, so it may be infeasible when the heap is large relative to the sample.
  - The estimand changes. It is now local to a population defined by a hole in its middle --- harder to describe, and further still from anything a policymaker asked about.
- Heaping is not fatal. But report both, with and without the donut, and let the reader see the difference.

# 6.5 Medicare and Universal Healthcare

## The question

- **Card, Dobkin and Maestas (2008)**: what does universal health insurance do to healthcare use? Medicare arrives sharply at age **65**.
- The stakes are large. In 2014 Medicare was $14\%$ of the US federal budget --- $\$505$ billion.
- Around $20\%$ of non-elderly US adults were uninsured in 2005, mostly from lower-income families, nearly half Black or Hispanic. Unequal coverage is a leading explanation for disparities in healthcare use and health outcomes.
- **Why observational comparisons fail.** Both the supply of and the demand for insurance depend on health status, so $\mathrm{cov}(u, C) \neq 0$. Comparing the insured with the uninsured measures selection as much as treatment --- and even among the insured, copays and deductibles vary with health.
- For the elderly the picture inverts: **under $1\%$ are uninsured**, most on fee-for-service Medicare, and the transition happens at one known age.

## The empirical design

Healthcare use $y$ depends on characteristics $C^k$ of coverage (copayments, generosity), for individual $i$, group $j$, age $a$. **$C$ is endogenous**, so OLS does not identify $\pi_k$:
$$
y_{ija} = X_{ija}\beta + f_j(a) + \textstyle\sum_k \pi_k C^k_{ija} + u_{ija}
$$

Model two coverage dummies --- any coverage, and generous coverage --- as jumping at 65, with $D_a = \mathbf{1}\{a \geq 65\}$:
$$
C^k_{ija} = X_{ija}\beta^k_j + g^k_j(a) + D_a\,\delta^k_j + v^k_{ija}, \qquad k = 1, 2
$$

Substituting, the jump in $y$ at 65 is a **combination** of the two coverage jumps: $\;\delta^y_j = \pi_1 \delta^1_j + \pi_2 \delta^2_j$.

- If $f_j$, $g^1_j$ and $g^2_j$ are all **continuous at 65** --- the identifying assumption --- any discontinuity in $y$ is due to insurance.
- One group gives one equation in two unknowns. With **several groups**, regressing $\delta^y_j$ on $\delta^1_j$ and $\delta^2_j$ across $j$ separates $\pi_1$ from $\pi_2$.

## The data

- **NHIS, 1992--2003.** Reports birth year, birth month, and calendar quarter of interview --- enough to construct **age in quarters**. Someone reaching 65 in the interview quarter is coded 65 and 0 quarters; assuming uniform interview dates, half of them are up to six weeks younger than 65 and half up to six weeks older.
- Restricted to ages 55--75. Final sample: **$160{,}821$** observations.
- **Hospital discharge records** for California, Florida and New York --- a complete census of discharges, with **age in months** at admission. Transfers dropped, ages 60--70 kept. Sample sizes $4{,}017{,}325$, $2{,}793{,}547$ and $3{,}121{,}721$.
- **The institution is genuinely sharp.** Coverage begins on the first day of the month you turn 65. Individuals are notified shortly before their birthday, and must enrol and choose whether to take Part B. Part A is free; Part B costs a modest premium.

## What jumps at 65: insurance

\begin{center}
\scriptsize
\begin{tabular}{lrrrrr}
\toprule
 & On Medicare & Any insurance & Private & 2+ forms & Managed care \\
\midrule
Overall sample        & $59.7$ & $9.5$  & $-2.9$ & $44.1$ & $-28.4$ \\
                      & $(4.1)$ & $(0.6)$ & $(1.1)$ & $(2.8)$ & $(2.1)$ \\[0.3em]
White, some college   & $68.4$ & $4.4$  & $-2.3$ & $55.1$ & $-40.1$ \\
                      & $(4.7)$ & $(0.5)$ & $(1.8)$ & $(4.0)$ & $(2.6)$ \\[0.3em]
Minority, HS dropout  & $44.5$ & $21.5$ & $-1.2$ & $19.4$ & $-8.3$ \\

\footnotesize
Percentage-point discontinuities at 65, from quadratics in age fully interacted with the post-65 dummy, plus controls for gender, education, race, region and year. Pooled 1999--2003 NHIS.
\normalsize

- The **first stage is enormous**: Medicare coverage jumps about $60$ points, and holding two or more forms of coverage jumps $44$.
- Who *gains* insurance and who merely **swaps** it differs sharply. Minority dropouts gain coverage ($+21.5$); white college-goers were already insured and mostly change its form ($+4.4$, with managed care down $40$ points).

## The confounder: what else happens at 65?

- Continuity requires that **everything else** trends smoothly through 65 --- observed and unobserved. But 65 is also the traditional retirement age, and non-workers have more time to visit a doctor.
- If employment fell discontinuously at 65, part of any jump in healthcare use would be leisure, not insurance.
- So the authors bring in a **third dataset**, the March CPS 1996--2004, and run the same RD with employment as the outcome. They find **no discontinuity at 65**.
- This is the covariate-balance logic of §6.4, aimed at the one confounder that institutional knowledge flags as dangerous.
- **The general lesson.** "Does anything else change at the cutoff?" is not a statistical question first. You answer it by knowing the institution, and then testing what that knowledge suggests. \hfill \emph{(added)}
